## File: SKILL.md

# Pitch decks

A deck is **spoken by a person and read by an audience at the same time**, which
is the whole problem: the two channels compete. Almost every bad deck is the
speaker's script pasted onto the slides.

This file is everything you need to build one. The `references/` folder holds the
reasoning and the citations, one file per task; read `references/INDEX.md` to
find the right one instead of loading them all.

## First, decide which artifact

A projected deck and an emailed deck are different products. Building one deck
for both jobs is the most common structural mistake, and the audit's thresholds
differ by `--mode` for exactly this reason.

| | Live, projected | Read-alone, emailed |
|---|---|---|
| Slides | about 10 | about 19 to 20 pages |
| Headline | 36 to 54 pt, default 42 | 30 to 44 pt, default 36 |
| Body | 24 to 30 pt, default 24 | 20 to 26 pt, default 22 |
| Labels and chart labels | 18 to 24 pt, default 20 | 16 to 20 pt, default 18 |
| Explanation | speaker notes | one short sentence on the slide |
| Appendix | handed over on request | attached behind the ask |

## The procedure

1. **Write the spine before opening any tool.** One line per slide, the claim
   the slide makes; if a line contains an "and", it is two slides. Read the
   spine back on its own: it must be the argument, not a table of contents,
   because layout cannot rescue a spine that argues nothing.
2. **Check the investor network's own rules first** and let them override
   everything here: required topics, slide cap, time limit, and what may not
   appear on a slide. Valuation is commonly forbidden.
3. **Give each slide one message and one hero object.** The hero is the largest
   thing on the slide. Everything else recedes.
4. **Move every sentence of explanation off the slide.** On a live deck it goes
   into the speaker notes, which are what you say anyway; on a read-alone deck
   there is no speaker, so it goes into the appendix. An emailed PDF carries no
   narration, notes nobody opens are the same as deleting the argument, and
   proof goes to the appendix in both cases.
5. **Emit the numbers from the source of truth into a data file** the build
   script reads. Never retype a figure onto a slide.
6. **Declare the grid and the palette once, as constants.** Every x and every
   width comes from the grid, never a typed offset.
7. **Build.** For `.pptx` write a build script on `python-pptx`, or use a pptx
   skill if one is installed. Hand-rolled geometry is where
   alignment drift and 48-object slides come from, because nothing checks the
   arithmetic.
8. **Charts native rather than drawn**, one axis, direct labels, the deck's own
   palette checked for contrast against **both** the light and the dark surface,
   with a `dataviz` skill's validator if one is installed or a WCAG contrast
   checker otherwise.
9. **Run the audit. Fix every finding. Re-run.**
10. **Render and look at it.** Convert to PDF, then to PNG, and view every page.
    The audit checks geometry, not whether the slide reads well.

## The enforced layer

```bash
python3 scripts/audit_deck.py deck.pptx                     # live deck
python3 scripts/audit_deck.py deck.pptx --mode read         # emailed deck
python3 scripts/audit_deck.py deck.pptx --minutes 5 --skip 11,12
```

It measures words per slide, objects per slide, smallest and largest type, size
contrast, hue families and tints, and near-miss edge alignment. It also flags
off-slide shapes, table columns wider than the slide, text-on-text overlap,
topic-label headlines, duplicate slide titles, centered body text and aspect
ratio. It checks whether the speaker notes can be said inside the time limit,
and it exits non-zero on any failure. `--skip` marks pages that are not projected slides, such as an
appendix: exempt from the projection limits and from the clock.

### Numeric thresholds

Each row is either sourced or marked JUDGMENT. A JUDGMENT row is a call made for
this skill: defensible, but do not present it to anyone as research.

| Check | Live | Read-alone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Words of on-slide text | 40 | 55 | JUDGMENT |
| Visible objects per slide | 6 | 6 | Phillips, below. His only. |
| Type floor | 18 pt | 14 pt | 18 pt: Harvard accessibility. 14 pt: JUDGMENT, **not** Harvard. |
| Largest type on a slide | 36 pt | 30 pt | the bottom of the sourced type scales, `references/04-type-and-layout.md` |
| Size contrast, largest over smallest | 1.8x | 1.8x | JUDGMENT |
| Hue families in the deck | 3 | 3 | JUDGMENT, from Tableau's "accent for emphasis, neutral elsewhere" |
| Tints inside one hue family | 3 | 3 | JUDGMENT |
| Near-miss edge alignment | 0.05 in | 0.05 in | JUDGMENT |
| Speaker notes | fit the clock at 110 wpm | not applicable | JUDGMENT, from the 8 to 12 minute guidance |

The 18 pt floor is the one row with real institutional weight behind it. The 14 pt
read-alone floor is a judgment: Harvard's figure is about type read across a
room, and a read-alone deck is read at desk distance.

### Non-numeric checks

The audit also fails a deck for an off-slide shape, a table whose columns sum
wider than the slide, or text overlapping text. It fails a slide title that is
a bare topic label, two slides with the same title, centered multi-line body
text, and an aspect ratio that is not 16:9.

**16:9 is a strong default, not a requirement.** The reference set names
legitimate exceptions. When one applies, pass the check explicitly rather than
arguing with it: it is the only check in the set that a correct deck can fail.

## The cognitive-load set

From David JP Phillips, "How to avoid death by PowerPoint", TEDxStockholmSalon.
It converges with the YC, MIT and Stanford guidance in `references/01-narrative.md`,
and `references/10-sources.md` grades how much weight each rule can carry. The six-object
figure is Phillips alone, and it is a talk rather than a cited experiment.

1. **One message per slide.** If the slide makes two points it is two slides.
2. **Six objects maximum.** Working memory holds about six objects, which is the
   same budget as one headline, zero to three supporting lines, one visual and
   one optional source line. A group counts as its members, because the eye sees
   the members; a native chart counts as one.
3. **Never make the audience read and listen at once.** Text on the slide and
   speech compete for one channel and neither lands.
4. **Size signals importance.** The most important element is the largest.
5. **Contrast directs the eye.** Dim rather than delete when a slide builds.
6. **Never read your slides aloud.**

## Non-negotiables

- **The headline is the conclusion, not the topic.** "Market" is a label;
  "Every professional already has a network, and none of them can search it"
  is a claim, illustrated in the manner of LinkedIn's 2004 deck. Read only the
  headlines in order: that sequence must be the argument.
- **If something only fits at 12 pt, the slide has too much on it.** The fix is
  never a smaller font: keep the source line at the floor size for the mode, and
  move only the overflow provenance to the appendix. On a live deck you say the
  provenance out loud, so the slide needs less; on a forwardable deck the source
  line is the only provenance the reader gets.
- **One sans-serif family**, with weight and size doing the work.
- **Count hue families, not hex values.** Counting hex values fails any deck with
  a two-tone chart while letting eleven shades of one blue pass as one color.
  Cluster by hue angle, budget the families, then budget the tints inside a
  family separately; neutrals are structure, not color, and do not count.
- **Validate the palette, do not eyeball it.** Use a contrast validator on
  both the light and the dark surface. A hue that passes on white
  can fail on a dark slide.
- **Left-align body text.** Center only covers, hero statements and big metrics.
- **Keep the frame constant and let the content zone vary.** Same headline
  position and size on every slide, different layout beneath it. Frame
  consistency is the credibility signal; zone variety is what stops the deck
  reading as a template.
- **Numbers read from the model, never retyped.**
- **The ask is a milestone story**, not a runway number.
- **No accent line under a title, and no decorative color bar or edge stripe**,
  including header bands, sidebar stripes, and thin accents along a card edge.
  Both read as machine-generated. Use a background tint, a shadow or whitespace.

## Fixing an existing deck

Run the audit first and keep the output. It turns "this looks bad" into a finite
list and tells you whether the fault is density, hierarchy, palette or geometry,
which need different fixes. Then rebuild from the build script rather than
patching the `.pptx`, because patched geometry drifts again on the next edit.

## The words themselves

This skill owns the surface: type, grid, palette, object count, density. The
`writing-style` skill owns the words, and it applies to every headline, body
line, source line and speaker note in the deck.

Where the two overlap they agree. An assertion headline is the same rule as a
claim-first sentence. The two things `writing-style` adds that this audit does
not measure: the banned machine-generated vocabulary, and one name per thing
reused across every slide rather than rotated for variety.

# House style

The defaults, in one page. If you do not want to make decisions, copy what is here.

This file holds defaults and owns no numbers. Every size, count and length lives in the file that sources it:

- Type, grid, alignment, aspect ratio: `04-type-and-layout.md`
- Color and contrast: `05-color-and-access.md`
- Which deck, how long, how many pages: `02-artifact-and-length.md`
- The thresholds the audit enforces: `../SKILL.md`

Where this page and one of those files appear to disagree, the other file wins.

---

## Canvas and artifact

- 16:9 widescreen is the strong default. `04-type-and-layout.md` lists the named exceptions.
- Exact canvas: 33.867 by 19.05 cm, PowerPoint widescreen, landscape.
- Send a PDF. Keep the `.pptx` as the live and editable master, so you can present from it and edit it without a round trip through the exported file.
- One deck does not serve every purpose. `02-artifact-and-length.md` owns the deck system, the slide counts and the read-alone page count.

---

## Typography

- One sans-serif family is the default. Two is the ceiling.
- An optional monospace face for code or technical identifiers does not spend the second slot.
- Semibold headlines, regular body. That single weight contrast carries the hierarchy without extra colors or rules.
- Sizes: use the two tables in the Typography section of `04-type-and-layout.md`, one for a live deck and one for a read-alone deck. Do not carry sizes over from this page; it does not list any.
- Nothing on a slide goes below the size floor for its mode. The floors, and which one is sourced and which one is a judgment, are stated in `04-type-and-layout.md`.

---

## Color

- Background: white or off-white, or a dark neutral. Pick one and hold it across the deck.
- Main text: near-black on light, near-white on dark.
- One brand color plus one accent covers most decks.
- Semantic colors, meaning positive, negative and warning, are a named exception to the hue-family cap. They are not an extra family competing for a slot, and they are not license to add decoration.
- The cap itself, how tints are counted, and the contrast targets live in `05-color-and-access.md`.

---

## Layout

- A consistent grid, reused on every slide. `04-type-and-layout.md` gives the working grid.
- Generous white space. Strong left alignment.
- One main visual zone per slide: a single chart, image, diagram or screenshot that the eye lands on. Two competing visual zones is the most common way a clean slide turns busy.
- A consistent footer and source treatment on every slide that needs one.
- No visual clutter: no drop shadows, no stray rules, no decorative shapes carrying no information.

### Source lines

Keep the source line on the slide, set at the size floor for the mode. Only overflow provenance, meaning the full citation, method notes and caveats, moves to the appendix.

The one case for dropping the on-slide source line is a live projected deck, where the presenter says the provenance out loud. Do not strip source lines from a deck that will be read alone.

---

## Content

- One conclusion per slide.
- Assertion-style titles: the title states the claim, not the topic.
- Evidence sits immediately under the claim it supports.
- Show the product visually rather than describing it.
- Bottom-up market sizing.
- Traction shown as a trend, not a single flattering number.
- A clear go-to-market, a clear business model, and honest competition.
- A milestone-based fundraising ask: what the money buys, not just how much.
- A large appendix, so the main sequence can stay short.

### Where the explanation goes

Split by mode. In a live deck, the explanation belongs in the speaker notes. In a read-alone deck it belongs in the appendix, because an emailed PDF carries no narration. Do not move detail into speaker notes for a deck nobody will present.

---

## Delivery

- A 30-second company explanation you can say from memory, with no slides.
- Core story length: see `02-artifact-and-length.md`.
- A longer version prepared, for the meeting that runs long or goes deep.
- Interruptions practiced, so a question in the middle does not derail the sequence.
- Key numbers memorized.
- An appendix you can search and jump into while talking. `07-delivery.md` covers the rehearsal detail.

# Narrative

What the deck has to argue, in what order, and how each slide title carries it.

## The Most Important Principle: Optimize for Understanding

Y Combinator’s presentation-design guidance emphasizes **legibility, simplicity, and obviousness**. YC also recommends focusing on only the handful of ideas an audience should remember.

Source:

- https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/how-to-design-a-better-pitch-deck

MIT Communication Lab independently recommends that **each slide convey one point** and that the slide title express the main takeaway.

Source:

- https://mitcommlab.mit.edu/broad/commkit/slideshow/

Stanford’s presentation guidance similarly recommends **one slide, one idea** and advises presenters to use visual aids for concepts that genuinely benefit from visuals rather than filling slides with speech text.

Source:

- https://oralcommprogram.stanford.edu/presentation-and-delivery/visuals-and-powerpoint

### Practical consequence

Do not ask:

> “How can I fit all of this on the slide?”

Ask:

> “What is the one thing the investor should understand after seeing this slide?”

If there are three independent conclusions, consider three slides.

---

## Investor Decks Are Internal-Selling Documents

A founder is rarely selling to only one person.

In many VC processes:

1. One investor meets the founder.
2. That investor summarizes the opportunity.
3. Other partners inspect the deck or an internal investment memo.
4. The firm discusses concerns.
5. The founder may present to a partner meeting.

First Round notes that the point partner commonly prepares an investment memo for other partners before a partner meeting.

Source:

- https://review.firstround.com/heres-what-you-can-really-expect-when-pitching-your-seed-stage-startup-at-a-vc-partner-meeting/

Andreessen Horowitz similarly describes diligence materials as inputs that help investors prepare internal investment discussions and memos.

Source:

- https://a16z.com/the-insiders-guide-to-data-rooms-what-to-know-before-you-raise/

### Design implication

Your deck should be easy for an investor to **retell accurately**.

A useful test:

> If an investor forwards the deck to a partner without you, can that partner correctly explain the company, problem, market, traction, business model, and reason to believe?

---

## Narrative Before Slides

Techstars’ 2026-05-07 guidance argues that founders often over-focus on deck production when the real product is the story. Its recommendation is to write the narrative before designing the slides.

Source:

- https://www.techstars.com/blog/founder-advice/why-most-pitch-decks-dont-work-and-how-to-make-sure-yours-does

### Recommended workflow

1. Write the investment story in prose.
2. Reduce it to approximately 5-7 memorable claims.
3. Put the claims in a logical sequence.
4. Turn each major claim into a slide headline.
5. Add evidence that proves each headline.
6. Remove any slide that does not advance the argument.
7. Build appendix slides for predictable objections.
8. Rehearse the story.
9. Only then refine visual design.

This sequencing is consistent with YC’s emphasis on a small set of memorable ideas.

Source:

- https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/how-to-design-a-better-pitch-deck

---

## Recommended Seed-Deck Architecture

DocSend’s updated 2026 seed guidance recommends a deck of approximately 19 to 20 pages containing 12 core sections.

Source:

- https://www.docsend.com/blog/what-vcs-really-want-to-see-inside-your-seed-deck/

Each section exists to answer one question an investor will ask anyway. A practical sequence is:

| Order | Section | Core question |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | Company purpose | What are you? |
| 2 | Problem | What important pain exists? |
| 3 | Solution | Why is your approach compelling? |
| 4 | Product | What actually exists? |
| 5 | Business model | Who pays, what do they pay, and what does it cost to serve? Then: how do you acquire customers, and how does usage become revenue and margin? |
| 6 | Market | Can this become large, and what can the company become if it succeeds? |
| 7 | Why now | Why is this opportunity newly possible or newly urgent? |
| 8 | Competition | What are the alternatives and why do you win? |
| 9 | Traction | What evidence proves demand? |
| 10 | Team | Why are you the team to build this? |
| 11 | Financials | What do the economics and runway look like? |
| 12 | Fundraising ask | What are you raising, and what will the new capital allow you to prove? |

Two positions in that table were moved from the sequence this document originally
carried, and both moves are argued in "Where the business model belongs" below.
Business model moved from 10 to 5, the position DocSend measured in decks that
raised. It now precedes Market, so the market number has units by the time the
reader meets it.

Product moved from 6 to 4 to stay next to it and in front of it. DocSend's reading
of the successful decks is that they couple product directly to monetization near
the front. Why now, Competition, Traction and Team each shifted down one and keep
their relative order, which no evidence speaks to either way.

The set of questions above is consistent with frameworks from Sequoia, Y Combinator, DocSend, NFX, Techstars, and First Round.

Sources:

- https://sequoiacap.com/article/writing-a-business-plan/
- https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/how-to-raise-a-seed-round/
- https://www.docsend.com/blog/what-vcs-really-want-to-see-inside-your-seed-deck/
- https://www.nfx.com/post/the-non-obvious-guide-to-fundraising
- https://www.techstars.com/blog/founder-advice/why-most-pitch-decks-dont-work-and-how-to-make-sure-yours-does
- https://review.firstround.com/heres-what-you-can-really-expect-when-pitching-your-seed-stage-startup-at-a-vc-partner-meeting/

DocSend reports that opening with company purpose, then problem, then solution, then market is associated with stronger fundraising outcomes in its dataset.

Source:

- https://www.docsend.com/blog/what-vcs-really-want-to-see-inside-your-seed-deck/

### Important caveat

Do not follow the sequence mechanically when your company has a stronger opening.

For example:

- A startup with extraordinary traction may lead with traction.
- A famous founder may use team earlier.
- A deep-tech company may need a brief technical breakthrough slide earlier.
- A highly visual consumer product may open with the product experience.

Techstars explicitly warns against treating decks as a paint-by-numbers exercise.

### Where the business model belongs, and the one thing anybody measured

The sequence above used to put business model at 10, which is the position
DocSend associates with decks that failed. It is now at 5. This subsection is
why.

DocSend's pre-seed report covered over 200 startups from 2022 to the first half of
2023. It found the business model section at position 4 in decks that raised and
position 10 in decks that did not. Its own reading is that successful founders
couple product directly to monetization at the front of the deck. This is the only
measurement anywhere of where a section actually sits in funded versus unfunded
decks, so it deserves more weight than any template.

DocSend's two datasets disagree with each other. The 2015 study with Harvard
Business School measured against a section order with business model at 8. Time on
the business model section also flips sign between reports: 94 percent more in
*successful* decks in one cohort, 233 percent more in *unsuccessful* decks in the
next. So time on
section is not a directional signal, and only the position finding is usable.

**The published templates split, roughly four to three for monetization before
market sizing:**

| Before market | After market |
|---|---|
| Y Combinator (BM 7, market 8) | Sequoia (BM 7, market 5, competition 6) |
| 500 Global (BM 6, competition 7, market 8) | Kawasaki (BM 8, sales 6, competition 7) |
| Founder Institute (BM 6, market 7) | |
| Techstars, Brohl (BM 6, market 7) | |
| CRV (BM 5, market 6) | |

Andreessen Horowitz publishes no slide order at all: every "a16z template" in
circulation is a third-party reconstruction by a deck vendor.

**The argument that does not depend on anyone's opinion is arithmetic.** A credible
bottom-up market number is price multiplied by customers. Put the market slide
first and you are asking the reader to accept a number whose units they have not
been given yet.

That objection gets sharper the further the payer sits from the user. In a B2B2C
model or a marketplace, the market slide is unreadable until the reader knows who
pays.

**Countervailing considerations.** Founder Institute states that the middle block,
roughly slides five through nine, is meant to be rearranged to fit the narrative.
Techstars writes that there is no definitive rule about order. Sequoia, the single
most copied template in the world, puts business model after both market and
competition.

At pre-seed the business model slide is a one-line monetization hypothesis, which
is cheap to place early. By Series A it is unit economics, which may need the
market established first.

**Evidence class.** No A/B test, randomized trial or controlled experiment on deck
section order exists in the public record. The largest dataset of funded versus
unfunded decks, 17,546 of them, has published nothing on order. The persuasion
literature supports putting strong material early for a high-elaboration audience
such as an investor
([Haugtvedt and Wegener 1994](https://academic.oup.com/jcr/article-abstract/21/1/205/1811820)),
but that is about argument order rather than deck sections. So: a defensible lean,
not a settled result.

One practical pressure points the same way. Average seed-deck first-read time has
fallen below two minutes in DocSend's 2023 cohort, and investor time per deck has
declined every year measured. The less time a reader gives you, the more expensive
it is to put anything load-bearing late.

Source:

- https://www.docsend.com/index/

Source:

- https://www.techstars.com/blog/founder-advice/why-most-pitch-decks-dont-work-and-how-to-make-sure-yours-does

## Use Assertion Headlines

MIT Communication Lab recommends titles that communicate the takeaway, not merely the subject.

Source:

- https://mitcommlab.mit.edu/broad/commkit/slideshow/

Harvard Catalyst similarly recommends beginning body slides with a strong headline.

Source:

- https://catalyst.harvard.edu/writing-communication-center/visualize-science/slides/

The same rule governs a chart’s headline, which states the chart’s conclusion rather than naming the measure; see `06-charts-and-data.md`.

### Weak to strong examples

| Weak title | Stronger title |
|---|---|
| Market | **$6.8B of annual spend is shifting to API-first platforms** |
| Problem | **Claims teams lose 11 hours per week to manual reconciliation** |
| Product | **One workflow replaces four disconnected tools** |
| Traction | **ARR grew 4.2× in twelve months while churn fell** |
| Competition | **Legacy vendors require 3× the implementation time** |
| Business model | **Expansion revenue lifts mature accounts above $40k ACV** |
| Team | **We spent 18 years building the infrastructure we are replacing** |
| Ask | **$3M gets us to enterprise repeatability and Series A readiness** |

### Headline-only test

Read only the slide titles in sequence.

If the titles do not form a coherent investment story, rewrite them.

---

## The Opening

Techstars’ 2026 storytelling guidance encourages founders to find an opening that creates genuine curiosity rather than beginning with generic company history.

Source:

- https://www.techstars.com/blog/founder-advice/why-most-pitch-decks-dont-work-and-how-to-make-sure-yours-does

### The techniques, with attribution

Deduplicated across Cicero, Conor Neill at IESE, Nancy Duarte, Chris Anderson at
TED, Carmine Gallo, Toastmasters, the MIT Communication Lab and Stanford. Every
modern list is a rediscovery of the classical exordium, and its three jobs organize
them better than any modern taxonomy. Those jobs are to make the audience
*attentus* (attentive), *docilis* (ready to learn) and *benevolus* (well disposed).

**Ordered best to worst for an INVESTOR pitch.** That ordering is not the one you
would use for a general audience, where the story open would sit first. It is built
from the unanimity of the investor-side sources below, which put identity before
any hook. Then comes the strength of the evidence behind each technique, then how
well it survives a hard time limit.

The running example is LinkedIn's Series B deck of August 2004, as annotated by Reid
Hoffman at https://www.reidhoffman.org/linkedin-pitch-to-greylock/. Every example
is an illustration written in the manner of that deck, not a line from it, and the
slide numbers are the ones printed on the slides.

| # | Opening | What it is | Example for LinkedIn, 2004 Series B | Class |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Declarative identity, then roadmap** | Name the company and what it does in one sentence, then the shape of what follows. No setup | Illustration: LinkedIn lets you find and contact the people you need through the people you already trust. In five minutes: the network, who pays for what sits on top, and the raise (slide 1) | B, and unanimous among investor sources |
| 2 | **Extraordinary number** | The one number that makes an investor sit up, said first. It needs a comparison the audience can picture, because a number they cannot scale is a number they discard | Illustration: The Series A plan promised about 400,000 users by now. The network has 900,000, growing 29,000 a week, on less than $4 million spent (slides 11, 14 and 16) | C |
| 3 | **Relevance open** | One sentence answering the unspoken "why should I care", before anything about you | Illustration: eBay, PayPal and Google each became valuable when a network replaced a flat directory. Professional people search is still a flat directory (slides 4 to 8) | B |
| 4 | **Narrative cold open** | Start mid-scene with one specific person at one moment, the way you would begin a story told to a child | Illustration: One member contacted ten product managers through their network and hired one (slide 26). Five founder stories are on file for other decks: see "The story bank" below | **A**, but see the investor caveat |
| 5 | **Contrast: what is versus what could be** | The status quo in the audience's own language, then the gap to a better future | Illustration: Today a professional is judged by their own claims in a resume database. On a network they are judged through the people who have worked with them (slides 3 and 8) | C |
| 6 | **Bold assertion of a contested view** | Your claim plus what is at stake, one sentence, no hedging | Illustration: Where the network is the asset, revenue comes second and the first mover wins. PayPal waited until 4 million users before turning on revenue (slide 9) | C |
| 7 | **Object or image reveal** | Put one artifact, image or short clip up and let it do the work | Illustration: Open on a live profile page and its connections, and say only that this is what a member sees. The deck itself used mockups of unbuilt products for the same job (slides 23, 25 and 28) | C |
| 8 | **Personal founder insight** | The thing you know that the room does not | Illustration: The founder's insight is that PayPal's fraud detection worked only once it saw the whole network of transactions. Professional reputation has the same shape (slides 6 and 34) | C |
| 9 | **Question** | See "Starting with a question" below: the form matters and so does the audience | Illustration, cover tagline plus our question: Your network is bigger than you think. Why can nobody search it? **Not for a five-minute pitch.** Better in a short elevator pitch, where attention is the vote | A, but conditional and the conditions run against this audience |
| 10 | **Dramatic silence** | Say nothing for several seconds so the room settles onto you | Generic: hold the Problem slide and say nothing for three seconds. **Caveat:** that is one percent of a five-minute hard stop | C, single source |
| 11 | **Quotation** | A short line from someone the audience already respects, chosen because it states your thesis better than you can | None advised for this deck; see the cautions below | C |

**The trap to avoid.** A famous line whose real origin undercuts it. "Insanity is
doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results" is
attributed to Einstein in countless decks. The earliest documented use is a 1981
newspaper account of a recovery-group meeting, and no Einstein source exists
([Quote Investigator](https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/03/23/same/)).

A room with one person who knows that is a room where the opening line has just
cost credibility instead of buying it. The general rule: if you cannot name the
publication and the year, do not use the quotation.

These were two rows until the examples showed they were not two techniques. "An
extraordinary metric" and "a surprising statistic" differ only in where the number
comes from. The second was really a delivery rule, anchor it to a comparison,
rather than a separate opening.

The sources agree: Conor Neill has one shocking factoid, and Y Combinator's "do not
bury the lead" is about ordering rather than a distinct device. So they are one
row, and the delivery rule is folded into it.

The extraordinary-number row must use a figure the deck itself can source. In the
LinkedIn example every figure comes from the annotated deck, with its slide number
beside it, so a reader can check each one in a minute. A world-scale statistic
borrowed from a third party has to meet the same bar.

### The story bank

Five public founder stories, logged so they can be reused instead of reconstructed
each time. Four are told by the founders themselves or documented by sources that
were read; the fifth is included because an insider disputes it.

**Read the Fit column first.** A story earns its place only when it shows the
mechanism the product sells. A moving story about something the product does not
do invites the obvious question of whether the product would have done it, and the
honest answer is no.

| Case | The story | The argument it makes | Fit | Status and source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Airbnb, 2007** (Brian Chesky and Joe Gebbia) | Two founders could not pay their rent. A design conference had sold out the city's hotels, so they offered airbeds and breakfast in their own apartment. In October 2007 three strangers slept on their floor and paid | The founders performed the core transaction by hand before any platform existed: spare space on one side, a stranded traveler on the other, money changing hands. A two-sided need, tested at the scale of one apartment | Shows the mechanism. It does not show trust, safety or payments, which came later | Founder told; see the sources below |
| **Dropbox, founded 2007** (Drew Houston) | Houston says he boarded a bus from Boston to New York, realized he had forgotten his thumb drive, and was annoyed because it kept happening. He opened his editor on the bus and started writing code | Names the exact pain the product removes, a file stranded on a device you do not have with you, and makes the founder the first user | Entry point, not the whole pitch. Houston and the 2007 Y Combinator application frame the product more broadly, as keeping a team's files in sync and backed up | Founder told, on Houston's word alone; see the sources below |
| **Slack, 2012** (Stewart Butterfield) | The game studio announced in November 2012 that its audience was too small to survive, and shut the servers on 2012-12-09. The core team had run on IRC and was living on a Slack prototype within a month | A team turned its own working habit into the product after the original plan failed. The internal communication setup was the one thing that worked | Shows the mechanism, with one correction: the prototype was built in a month on habits formed in IRC, not a finished internal tool released as is | Documented; see the sources below |
| **Spanx, 1998 to 2000** (Sara Blakely) | In 1998 Blakely wanted a smooth line under white pants for a party and cut the feet off her control-top pantyhose. Two years of prototypes followed. She launched with $5,000 in savings and ran every role from her apartment | The improvised prototype is the product. The story shows the exact use case and a fix the audience can picture in one step; the $5,000 and the one-woman operation show bootstrapping | Shows the mechanism. The sources read stop before the patent and the first retail deal, so the story stops there too | Founder told; see the sources below |
| **Netflix, 1997** (Reed Hastings tells it; Marc Randolph disputes it) | Hastings has told the story of a rented VHS returned six weeks late and a $40 fee as the spark for Netflix. In some tellings the film is Apollo 13 | A tidy epiphany that sells the product's benefit, no late fees, in one scene | Fails the fit test. Co-founder Marc Randolph says the idea had nothing to do with late fees, and Netflix charged late fees at launch; the subscription model came more than 18 months later | Disputed by a co-founder; see the sources below |

**Sources for the story bank.** One bullet per case, in table order.

- Airbnb: Chesky's own article, 2014-07-16, https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/20140716195656-13378252-belong-anywhere. The company's timeline, https://news.airbnb.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2018/08/The-Airbnb-Story-Timeline-EN-GLOBAL.pdf, puts the first stay in fall 2007, and its newsroom, https://news.airbnb.com/about-us, in October 2007. The sold-out conference is from Gebbia's TED talk of 2016, read in a third-party transcript at singjupost.com.
- Dropbox: the company's post quoting Houston, https://www.linkedin.com/posts/dropbox_what-inspired-drew-houston-to-start-dropbox-activity-7310714989898571777-qS9F. The bus quote is in Fortune, 2017-06-14, https://fortune.com/2017/06/14/founder-dropbox-got-idea-chinatown-bus/, citing a Business Insider podcast. The 2007 Y Combinator application, https://www.ycombinator.com/apply/dropbox, frames the product more broadly, does not mention the bus, and no source dates the trip.
- Slack: the closure and the layoffs, Game Developer, 2012-11-15, https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/tiny-speck-s-unsustainable-mmo-i-glitch-i-closes-down. The IRC setup and the one-month prototype, Johnny Rodgers's first-person account, https://buildingslack.com/the-death-of-glitch-the-birth-of-slack/.
- Spanx: Blakely's post for the 19th anniversary, October 2019, https://www.linkedin.com/posts/sarablakely27_entrepreneur-business-activity-6590603808496238592-mGRM. The $5,000 is in her article of 2020-04-03, https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/why-im-giving-5m-help-female-entrepreneurs-sara-blakely. The 1998 party and the two years of prototypes are on https://spanx.com/pages/about-us.
- Netflix: Hastings's telling, CBS 60 Minutes, 2006-12-01, https://www.cbsnews.com/news/the-brain-behind-netflix/. Randolph's dispute, WBUR On Point, 2019-11-07, https://www.wbur.org/onpoint/2019/11/07/netflix-marc-rudolph-that-will-never-work, his book *That Will Never Work* (2019), and his posts https://www.linkedin.com/posts/marcrandolph_the-idea-of-the-epiphany-is-a-myth-there-activity-7156350579898806272-cEij and https://www.linkedin.com/posts/marcrandolph_ok-reed-ive-got-another-one-personalized-activity-7051730646834049024-EQXO. The 18-month timing is on https://marcrandolph.com/25years/.

The Netflix row is the teaching point. The late-fee story feels right and sells the
benefit, and an insider still contradicts it. Randolph, the co-founder and first
CEO, says the idea did not come from late fees
([WBUR On Point, 2019-11-07](https://www.wbur.org/onpoint/2019/11/07/netflix-marc-rudolph-that-will-never-work)).
A pitch opening has to survive a fact check by the people in the room, and a
co-founder is one of them.

Two honesty notes that apply to the set as a whole:

- **A story is one case, not evidence.** Say that this is what happened to one
  founder once, not that it proves the market or the model.
- **A story that a checkable source contradicts costs more than it buys.** One
  person in the room who knows the contradiction makes the opening cost
  credibility instead of earning it, and every later slide is read with more
  suspicion.

### The figure bank, and a worked example of how a number drifts

Companion to the story bank. A headline figure gets reused across a deck, an
application and a website, and once it drifts it drifts everywhere at once. The
worked example below is invented, because the mechanism is the lesson.

**What holds up.** A figure holds up when the cited page contains the cited number
and the number is scoped to what the company sells. It helps when the raw extract
behind it sits beside the document that uses it.

**A made-up case, with made-up numbers.** A deck says 40 percent of a market is
addressable and footnotes an industry report. The report says 40 percent of the
online segment is addressable, and the online segment is a quarter of the market.
The honest figure is 10 percent.

**What does not hold up:**

- The deck and the report describe different quantities, and the page behind the
  footnote does not contain the number the deck attributes to it.
- A reader who clicks the footnote finds a different statistic. That is the worst
  available failure mode in front of a diligence reader.
- The company's own appendix already carried the 10 percent, correctly scoped.
  Somewhere between two documents the word online was lost, and the number
  quadrupled.

**The drift, traced end to end.** Recalled later from memory, the figure shrank
again to a third value on a slide. So the deck and the chart disagreed, neither
number could be derived from the footnote, and the right number had been in an
internal document the whole time.

The lesson is not "check your sources". It is "check whether you already have the
answer". The failure was not research; a scoped figure moved from one document to
another and shed its scope on the way.

**The fix was not to correct the smaller number upward to the larger one.** The
larger number inherited the lost scope, so it was the weaker claim. The fix was to
put back the figure that is sourced, checkable and scoped to what the product sells.

**Keep the raw extract, not just the number.** Store the export behind the
corrected figure beside the appendix that uses it, unzipped so it is greppable and
diffable. Add a README stating what it does and does not establish. A figure whose
source data is one directory away is a figure nobody has to re-search.

**Four transferable lessons:**

1. **Scope the headline figure to what you actually sell.** A figure about the
   whole field invites the question of why you only cover part of it. A figure
   scoped to your part answers it in the same breath.
2. **A figure that cannot survive a click on its own footnote is worse than no
   figure.** Check that the cited page contains the cited number, every time.
3. **The bigger number is not the stronger one.** It is the one whose derivation
   holds.
4. **Search your own files before searching the web.** The correctly scoped figure
   already existed internally. Every hour spent re-deriving it was spent because
   nobody knew it was there, which is an argument for one evidence document per
   claim-heavy slide rather than per pitch.

### A story is owned by whoever can say "I"

Consent and deliverability are two different questions, and the second one decides
which story to use.

Chesky and Gebbia can tell the Airbnb story as "we", because they were in the
apartment. Anyone else telling it is reporting. In their mouths it is our first
three guests; in anyone else's it becomes the founders' first three guests, which
is a materially weaker thing. The speaker is now reporting rather than testifying,
and the room can hear the difference.

That matters because many pitch formats allow one presenter for both the short
elevator pitch and the longer pitch. So the presenter's own story is the only
first-person option, and every borrowed story is second-hand.

**Which to use where, given that:**

- **The presenter's own story, in both formats.** It is the only first-person
  option, it needs nobody's permission, and it should demonstrate a mechanism
  rather than a misfortune. Spanx is the model: only Blakely can say she cut the
  feet off her own pantyhose.
- **A two-founder story, when either founder presents.** Airbnb is the model:
  Chesky or Gebbia can testify to hosting three strangers in their own apartment;
  a hired presenter can only report it.
- **A co-founder's story, only when that co-founder presents.** Dropbox is the
  model: the bus and the forgotten drive are Houston's. Told second-hand it still
  works, but say plainly whose story it is rather than blurring it.
- **A documented team story, wherever the objection is that the plan might
  fail.** Slack is the model: the studio's own announcement documents the failure,
  so the pivot needs nobody's testimony and anyone can tell it.
- **A disputed story: the appendix at most, and better nowhere.** Netflix is the
  model: an insider contradicts the mechanism, so it cannot open a pitch. If it
  comes up from the floor, name the dispute.

**Rows 4 and 9 are inverted on purpose.** The story open has the best experimental
support of any technique and ranks fourth here. The question open also has genuine
experimental support and ranks ninth.

Both are demoted for the same reason, which is the audience. The investor-side
sources are unanimous that identity comes before any hook, and the
rhetorical-question effect reverses against a high-involvement audience. Neither
is a weak technique; they are strong techniques aimed at a different room.

**The story open is the only one with direct experimental support for the opening
position specifically** (Andeweg, de Jong and Hoeken, *Technical Communication
Quarterly* 7(3), 1998). It is also the only technique recommended by every
independent source surveyed, and it tops the one catalog that counted. Andeweg and
de Jong went through 136 twentieth-century Dutch-language speaking manuals and
narrowed them to 42 with expert help. The anecdote was the most recommended
attention-getter.

One honest caveat on the whole table. Van De Mieroop, de Jong and Andeweg analyzed
the introductions of 40 engineering speeches (*Journal of Business and Technical
Communication*, 2008). Real expert speakers mostly do not use the technique the
manuals recommend most. Either the advice is wrong or the field
ignores good advice, and nobody has established which.

### Starting with a question

This technique needs its condition attached. It is one of the few presentation
techniques with a real experimental literature, and that literature is
conditional.

Conor Neill of IESE Business School teaches it as one of his three main openings,
and ranks it third, behind the story and the shocking factoid. He defines it as
phrasing the problem the audience already lives with as a question they cannot
answer comfortably.
([IESE](https://www.iese.edu/standout/how-to-start-speech/))

**Three forms, and the experiments found different results for each. Do not
conflate them.**

1. **Rhetorical question.** No answer expected; the only sensible answer supports
   you. This is the measured form.
2. **Hypophora.** You ask, then answer it yourself within a sentence or two, so it
   works as a curiosity gap rather than a request for agreement. Zillmann and
   Cantor (*British Journal of Educational Psychology*, 1973) found improved recall
   of the facts presented, chiefly when attention was otherwise low.
3. **Prequestion.** You ask the question your talk will answer, then answer it over
   the talk. Reliably improves learning of the specific information the question
   addressed, less reliably anything else, with no detriment found.
4. **Genuine show of hands.** Practitioner advice only. No experiment tests it as
   an opening.

**The condition that matters: a question only helps an audience that was not
already thinking hard.**

A rhetorical question works by making people think harder about what you just
said. That is worth something when they were half paying attention. It is worth
nothing when they were already concentrating, and it can actively get in the way.

Petty, Cacioppo and Heesacker (*JPSP* 40(3), 1981) tested exactly that. They gave
people an argument, phrased either as plain statements or as rhetorical questions,
and varied how much the topic personally affected them. When the topic barely
affected them, the questions made them engage more, so a strong argument landed
better and a weak one landed worse. When the topic affected them a great deal, they
described the questions as distracting, and they engaged with the argument less
than the people who got plain statements.

An investor deciding whether to give you money is the second case. They are already
paying as much attention as they have. A question cannot raise attention that is
already at the ceiling, so the only thing it can do is spend some of it.

Two things partly rescue it. Burnkrant and Howard (*JPSP* 47(6), 1984) reran the
same message with the questions moved to the introduction rather than after each
argument, and in print rather than spoken. They reported enhanced elaboration
regardless of relevance. So an introductory question in a document the reader
controls is a different and safer proposition than a spoken rhetorical question
mid-argument.

Treat that as Petty and Cacioppo's reading of the study rather than verified from
the primary text.

**Where it backfires:**

- **Once the audience notices the question as a device.** Ahluwalia and Burnkrant
  (*JCR* 31(1), 2004) show that high salience of the rhetorical form redirects
  elaboration away from your argument and onto you as a persuasion agent.
- **In front of a weak argument.** Every experiment crossing question form with
  argument quality found the same asymmetry: raising elaboration amplifies
  whatever comes next, in both directions. A question opening is a bet on the
  strength of what follows.
- **Repeated through the talk.** Munch and Swasy (1988) found rhetoricals reduced
  argument recall, worse with frequency.
- **Delivered with rhetorical intonation.** The only experiment set in a sales
  pitch had 72 listeners rate speakers, including on the probability of investing
  (Neitsch and Niebuhr, *Journal of Psycholinguistic Research* 51(5), 2022).
  Delivery dominated wording, and rhetorical-question prosody lowered speaker
  ratings.
- **As a show of hands with a small, senior or unfamiliar audience**, where a
  non-response is the likely outcome and there is no recovery.
- **In writing, on a title slide or a subject line**, where the reader is still
  deciding whether to engage at all. Question framing measurably hurts there,
  across 53,030 Reddit posts, more than three million academic articles, 22,743
  headline A/B tests and a preregistered experiment.

Honest limit: no experiment in this literature used investors, funding decisions or
a live pitch. The high-involvement condition was undergraduates facing a graduation
requirement.

### The investor audience is different, and the sources are unanimous

This is where general presentation coaching and investor-side advice pull apart,
and for a funding pitch the investor side wins.

Every named investor-side source says open by stating plainly what the company
does, with no preamble and no problem setup:

- Michael Seibel and Kevin Hale at Y Combinator, who say to skip the problem setup
  and get to the point, and Geoff Ralston on demo day.
- Sequoia's own template ("define your company in a single declarative sentence").
- Reid Hoffman's annotated LinkedIn Series B deck: "I now believe you should begin
  and end with the investment thesis"
  ([reidhoffman.org](https://www.reidhoffman.org/linkedin-pitch-to-greylock/)).

The one accelerator that does advocate a hook, Techstars via Nicole Glaros, names
five devices, and a question is not among them.

The research explains why rather than leaving it as a style preference:

- **Experts want concrete "how", novices want abstract "why".** Falchetti, Cattani
  and Ferriani (*Strategic Management Journal*, 2022, four experiments) found that
  lay evaluators and crowdfunders respond to abstract framing. Expert evaluators
  respond to concrete framing of how the thing works.
- **Investors fund perceived preparedness, not displayed passion.** Chen, Yao and
  Kotha (*AMJ*, 2009), lab experiment plus a field study of real business-plan
  competitions.
- **The mechanism is cognitive legitimacy**, meaning the evaluator understands what
  the business is. Pollack, Rutherford and Nagy (*ETP*, 2012) coded 113 funded
  pitches across Shark Tank and Dragons' Den.
- **Expert evaluators categorize you in the first seconds and weight negative cues
    heavily**, and pitchers do not recover. Elsbach and Kramer (*AMJ*, 2003) studied
  28 Hollywood pitch meetings in the field; the cues that sank a pitch included
  seeming too slick, formulaic, or pitching by rote. Conversely, openings that got
  the evaluator contributing their own ideas raised their judgment of the pitcher.
- **In a short competition format, delivery outruns wording.** Tsay (*Academy of
  Management Discoveries*, 2021, 12 studies, 1,855 participants) tested 60-second
  pitches. Six seconds of silent video from the start predicted the investors'
  actual picks better than the audio did.
- **Your slot in the running order matters and your opening cannot fix it.**
  Clingingsmith, Conley and Shane (*Journal of Innovation Economics and
  Management*, 2022) randomized position across four university elevator-pitch
  competitions: pitching early scored lower.

### What to avoid

- **Preamble**: thanks, self-introduction, agenda, credentials. Every authority says
  no, and it remains the most common opening in real professional practice.
- **A joke.** Most attempted jokes in a professional talk do not land, and a failed
  one is not neutral: it signals lower competence and costs status. Borrowed humor
  is worse, because the same words carry differently out of a different mouth.
- **A statistic with no comparison.** A number the audience cannot scale is a
  number they discard.
- **Story, problem setup or category-shift framing before the audience can name
  your business.** Hook first is general advice; for investors, identity first.

### Then, immediately

The opening should still lead rapidly to:

> What the company does and why it matters.

---

---

# Which deck, how long

A projected deck and an emailed deck are different products. Slide count, length and stage follow from which one you are building.

## Build a Deck System, Not One Universal Deck

One of the biggest improvements to pitch-deck practice is to stop treating “the deck” as a single artifact.

Techstars’ current fundraising-material guidance distinguishes several materials for different moments in the process.

Source:

- https://www.techstars.com/blog/founder-advice/techstars-fundraising-series-prepping-your-materials

### Recommended deck ecosystem

#### A. Forwardable / emailable deck

Purpose:

- Get the meeting.
- Be understandable without the founder present.
- Travel internally inside an investment firm.
- Make the company easy to summarize to another partner.

Characteristics:

- Concise.
- Self-contained.
- Slightly more explanatory text than a live deck.
- Strong company-purpose slide.
- Clear proof points.
- Minimal confidential detail.
- No animations required for comprehension.

Techstars’ toolkit notes that founders commonly use **PDF or controlled document-sharing links** for emailable decks.

Source:

- https://toolkit.techstars.com/build-your-investor-pipeline

#### B. Meeting deck

Purpose:

- Guide a discussion.
- Provide visual anchors.
- Allow the founder to control sequencing without turning the meeting into a lecture.

Characteristics:

- Larger type.
- More visual.
- Less body text.
- Designed to survive interruptions.
- Strong navigation and section logic.

Techstars describes the investor meeting deck as a narrative presentation and advises founders to expect interruptions.

Source:

- https://www.techstars.com/blog/founder-advice/techstars-fundraising-series-prepping-your-materials

#### C. Drill-down / appendix deck

Purpose:

- Answer detailed investor questions immediately.
- Demonstrate command of metrics and operating details.
- Support partner meetings and diligence.

Possible appendix slides:

- Cohort retention
- Revenue concentration
- Sales pipeline
- CAC detail
- LTV assumptions
- Gross margin evolution
- Product roadmap
- Hiring plan
- Competitive landscape
- Market calculation
- Funnel conversion
- Customer segmentation
- Pricing sensitivity
- Financial assumptions
- Security/regulatory detail where relevant

First Round specifically recommends having a large appendix available in partner meetings and gives examples such as cohort analysis, competitive landscape, customer revenue breakdown, and sales pipeline.

Source:

- https://review.firstround.com/heres-what-you-can-really-expect-when-pitching-your-seed-stage-startup-at-a-vc-partner-meeting/

#### D. Data room

The deck is not the data room.

Andreessen Horowitz describes the pitch deck as only one part of diligence alongside items such as cap table, historical P&L, burn, and other supporting documents.

Source:

- https://a16z.com/the-insiders-guide-to-data-rooms-what-to-know-before-you-raise/

---

## Stage-Specific Differences

### Pre-seed

At pre-seed, the deck often needs to prove:

- Founder insight
- Problem importance
- Why now
- Early user/customer discovery
- Product insight/prototype
- Market potential
- Team-market fit
- Credible first milestones

DocSend’s updated **2026-02-24** pre-seed research reports investors spending approximately **4 minutes 10 seconds** reviewing a pre-seed deck on average.

Source:

- https://www.docsend.com/blog/what-to-include-when-building-your-pre-seed-pitch-deck/

#### Pre-seed emphasis

More:

- Insight
- Founder credibility
- Product vision
- Customer evidence
- Why now

Less:

- Long financial histories
- Mature unit economics
- Over-engineered five-year forecasts

### Seed

At seed, stronger evidence is normally expected:

- Repeatable usage
- Early revenue or strong demand signals
- Growth
- Retention
- Distribution learning
- Business-model clarity
- Capital efficiency

DocSend’s 2026 seed research emphasizes capital efficiency, realistic projections, a path toward sustainable economics, and evidence-backed claims.

Source:

- https://www.docsend.com/blog/what-vcs-really-want-to-see-inside-your-seed-deck/

### Series A

At Series A, the deck should usually demonstrate:

- Product-market fit
- Meaningful scale
- Growth consistency
- Cohort/retention evidence
- A scalable GTM motion
- Unit economics
- Hiring ability
- Defensibility
- A credible route to a very large outcome

NFX’s Series A framework emphasizes traction, PMF, scalability, unit economics, vision, defensibility, and a world-class presentation of data.

Source:

- https://www.nfx.com/post/fundraising-checklist-13-proof-points-series-a

---

## Slide Count

There is no universal correct number.

Different credible sources recommend different constraints because they describe different artifacts.

Slide count is a property of the artifact, not of the company. The same company can be right at ten live slides and right again at twenty sent pages, because the two products do different work. For which artifacts exist and what each one is for, see "Build a Deck System, Not One Universal Deck" above.

### What the sources say

#### DocSend seed research

Approximately **19-20 pages** for a full seed deck. That figure is the DocSend dataset number. Do not widen it into a rounder band unless you label the wider band a judgment of your own.

Source:

- https://www.docsend.com/blog/what-vcs-really-want-to-see-inside-your-seed-deck/

#### Guy Kawasaki

Ten slides, as the slide-count half of the 10/20/30 heuristic covered below.

Source:

- https://guykawasaki.com/the-only-10-slides-you-need-in-your-pitch/

#### Techstars

Current fundraising-material guidance describes a meeting deck intended to tell the story in a short presentation and expects interruptions.

Source:

- https://www.techstars.com/blog/founder-advice/techstars-fundraising-series-prepping-your-materials

### Guy Kawasaki 10/20/30

Guy Kawasaki’s famous heuristic is:

- 10 slides
- 20 minutes
- 30-point minimum type

Source:

- https://guykawasaki.com/the-only-10-slides-you-need-in-your-pitch/

It is useful as a discipline for live pitches, especially when a deck is becoming bloated.

It is a heuristic, and it must not override:

- DocSend’s longer read-alone seed decks.
- First Round’s partner-meeting appendix guidance.
- Techstars’ multi-deck system.
- The type scale in `04-type-and-layout.md`. Kawasaki’s 30 pt is a floor for live body copy, not a license to set headlines at 30 pt. Take headline and body sizes from the two tables in that file.

---

## Live Pitch Length

500 Global recommends keeping initial investor presentations under roughly 20 minutes and leaving substantial time for discussion.

Source:

- https://500.co/content/top-19-insights-on-startup-fundraising-in-a-remote-environment

Techstars’ current materials guidance describes a shorter meeting narrative and emphasizes expecting interruptions.

Source:

- https://www.techstars.com/blog/founder-advice/techstars-fundraising-series-prepping-your-materials

### Slides per minute

Harvard gives a general live-presentation heuristic of approximately one slide per minute.

Source:

- https://hsph.harvard.edu/research/health-communication/resources/slide-checklist/

That is a general presentation heuristic and it does not apply to an investor pitch. An investor meeting is interrupted, the running order bends to the questions asked, and a single slide can hold the screen for several minutes of discussion. Use it to sanity-check a lecture or a conference talk, not to size a pitch deck.

### Practical default

For a scheduled 30-minute meeting:

- 8-12 minutes prepared core story
- Remaining time discussion

For a 60-minute partner meeting:

- Prepare a core version and a longer version
- Expect interruptions
- Keep appendix ready

First Round specifically recommends practicing both short and long versions.

Source:

- https://review.firstround.com/heres-what-you-can-really-expect-when-pitching-your-seed-stage-startup-at-a-vc-partner-meeting/

### Enforced (see SKILL.md)

The speaker notes are the script, so they are checkable against the clock. Pass the length you actually have, for example the 10 minutes at the middle of the prepared core story above:

```bash
python3 scripts/audit_deck.py deck.pptx --minutes 10
```

Notes word count divided by 110 words a minute. If the notes do not fit, the
pitch does not fit, and a moderator with a hard stop will cut you off mid
sentence. Aim at about 85% of the limit so there is room to breathe, and note
that spelled-out numbers cost real speaking time.

---

# Slide by slide

What belongs on each slide, what a strong version looks like, and what to avoid.

## Slide-by-Slide Recommendations

### 9.1 Cover / company-purpose slide

#### Must answer

> What do you do?

#### Recommended content

- Logo/name
- One-sentence description
- Optional product visual or customer outcome
- Optional key proof point if genuinely remarkable

#### Better one-liner structure

> **[Company] helps [specific customer] achieve [valuable outcome] by [distinct mechanism].**

Alternative:

> **We automate [specific task] for [specific customer], reducing [pain/cost/time] by [measurable result].**

Sequoia recommends defining the company in a single declarative sentence.

Source:

- https://sequoiacap.com/article/writing-a-business-plan/

NFX also has extensive guidance around capturing the essence of a business in one sentence.

Source:

- https://www.nfx.com/post/the-nfx-pitch-deck-library

#### Avoid

- “AI-powered next-generation platform”
- “Revolutionizing the future of X”
- Multiple unexplained category terms
- Mission statements that do not explain the product

---

### 9.2 Problem

#### Must answer

> Is this a painful, frequent, expensive, risky, or strategically valuable problem?

Strong evidence includes:

- Customer behavior
- Current workflow
- Existing spend
- Time wasted
- Revenue lost
- Regulatory risk
- Failure rates
- Customer interviews
- Customer quotes summarized rather than overused
- Existing workaround costs

Sequoia recommends describing the customer pain and current solutions/shortcomings.

Source:

- https://sequoiacap.com/article/writing-a-business-plan/

#### Better headline

Weak:

> **Problem**

Strong:

> **Finance teams still spend 14 hours each week reconciling fragmented data**

The second headline gives the investor a claim to evaluate.

---

### 9.3 Solution

#### Must answer

> What changed for the customer?

Show:

- Before vs after
- Workflow reduction
- Speed improvement
- Cost reduction
- Quality increase
- New capability
- Risk reduction

Do not turn the solution slide into a feature matrix.

The best solution slide normally explains the outcome first and the mechanism second.

---

### 9.4 Why now

Sequoia explicitly includes “Why now?” in its framework.

Source:

- https://sequoiacap.com/article/writing-a-business-plan/

NFX also emphasizes timing as central to startup narratives.

Sources:

- https://www.nfx.com/post/the-nfx-pitch-deck-library
- https://www.nfx.com/post/fundraising-checklist-13-proof-points-series-a

A strong “why now” can come from:

- New regulation
- Cost collapse
- Platform shift
- AI/model capability
- Hardware availability
- Consumer behavior change
- Distribution change
- New data availability
- Demographic shift
- Market consolidation
- Legacy technology reaching a breaking point

#### Avoid

Generic trend charts that are only loosely connected to the startup.

---

### 9.5 Market

#### Strong method

Use a bottom-up market model where possible:

> Number of realistic customers × annual spend per customer = addressable opportunity

NFX recommends bottom-up TAM thinking.

Source:

- https://www.nfx.com/post/the-non-obvious-guide-to-fundraising

DocSend’s updated seed guidance also warns against inflated market claims and recommends clearly identifying the initial customer segment.

Source:

- https://www.docsend.com/blog/what-vcs-really-want-to-see-inside-your-seed-deck/

#### Useful market layers

- **Beachhead**: first segment you can win
- **SAM**: practical serviceable market
- **TAM**: long-run total potential
- **Expansion**: adjacent segments/products

#### Avoid

> “The global software market is $800B. If we capture 1%, we are an $8B business.”

This shows arithmetic, not a go-to-market thesis.

---

### 9.6 Product

YC recommends graphics, charts, and screenshots over large quantities of words.

Source:

- https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/how-to-raise-a-seed-round/

DocSend’s 2026 guidance recommends showing the product clearly rather than describing it abstractly.

Source:

- https://www.docsend.com/blog/what-vcs-really-want-to-see-inside-your-seed-deck/

#### Good product slide

- One screenshot
- One highlighted workflow
- One sentence explaining the user value
- One proof point

#### Better than

- Full-screen UI screenshot
- 12 tiny annotations
- 8 feature cards
- Unreadable navigation chrome

---

### 9.7 Traction

Useful evidence can include:

- Revenue
- ARR/MRR
- Revenue growth
- Gross margin
- Active users
- Paid users
- Retention
- Cohort behavior
- Engagement
- Usage frequency
- Conversion
- Pipeline
- Pilots
- Signed contracts
- LOIs
- Waitlist
- Product usage
- Expansion revenue
- Renewal
- Customer references

#### Principle

Show trend, scale and quality.

A number without context is weak.

For example:

Weak:

> 1,000 customers

Stronger:

> 1,000 paid customers, up from 240 twelve months ago, with 92% annual retention

NFX’s Series A guidance emphasizes consistent month-to-month growth, retention/PMF evidence, and scale.

Source:

- https://www.nfx.com/post/fundraising-checklist-13-proof-points-series-a

#### Avoid vanity metrics

Examples:

- Page views without conversion
- Waitlist size without activation
- Downloads without retention
- Social impressions
- Cumulative signups when active usage is weak

---

### 9.8 Go-to-market / distribution

This slide answers:

> How does the company acquire customers repeatedly?

Include:

- Initial ICP
- Channel
- Sales cycle
- Conversion
- Acquisition motion
- ACV/AOV
- CAC where meaningful
- Payback where meaningful
- Expansion motion
- Partnerships where important

NFX explicitly includes distribution in its recommended pitch-deck elements.

Source:

- https://www.nfx.com/post/the-non-obvious-guide-to-fundraising

---

### 9.9 Business model

DocSend’s 2026 seed guidance reports particularly high investor attention on business-model content and emphasizes clear paths toward sustainable economics.

Source:

- https://www.docsend.com/blog/what-vcs-really-want-to-see-inside-your-seed-deck/

Answer:

- Who pays?
- What do they buy?
- How much do they pay?
- How frequently?
- What drives expansion?
- What gross margin is possible?
- What are the cost drivers?
- What happens at scale?

#### Good visual formats

- Pricing ladder
- Unit-economics bridge
- Customer economics
- Revenue equation
- Gross-margin evolution
- Simple funnel

#### Avoid

A screenshot of a spreadsheet.

---

### 9.10 Competition / alternatives

Sequoia recommends discussing direct and indirect competition.

Source:

- https://sequoiacap.com/article/writing-a-business-plan/

Competition includes:

- Direct startups
- Incumbents
- Internal/manual workflows
- Consultants
- Spreadsheets
- “Do nothing”
- Adjacent software

#### Strong competitive slides

- Comparison based on criteria customers care about
- Market map with clear axes
- Workflow comparison
- Cost/time/outcome comparison
- Positioning based on defensible strengths

#### Weak competitive slides

- Your logo alone in the upper-right corner of a 2×2
- Competitors intentionally placed on irrelevant axes
- “No competition”
- A wall of logos with no insight

---

### 9.11 Defensibility

Potential sources of defensibility:

- Network effects
- Proprietary data
- Distribution advantage
- Scale economies
- Workflow embedding
- Switching costs
- Regulatory position
- Brand
- Unique supply
- Technical advantage
- Learning loops

NFX stresses defensibility strongly in Series A fundraising.

Source:

- https://www.nfx.com/post/fundraising-checklist-13-proof-points-series-a

Avoid using “moat” as a label without showing how the advantage compounds.

---

### 9.12 Team

#### Answer

> Why are these people unusually likely to solve this problem?

Show relevance, not full biographies.

Useful proof:

- Domain insight
- Prior company-building
- Technical credibility
- Customer access
- Unique research
- Distribution expertise
- Prior collaboration
- Relevant outcomes
- Exceptional recruiting

NFX emphasizes the ability to attract talent as a positive signal at later stages.

Source:

- https://www.nfx.com/post/fundraising-checklist-13-proof-points-series-a

#### Better format

**Name, role.** One sentence explaining the relevant unfair advantage.

#### Avoid

- Full LinkedIn histories
- University logos with no relevance
- 12 advisors
- Tiny bios
- Vanity credentials without a connection to execution

---

### 9.13 Financials

At early stage, the financial slide should explain the economic model, not pretend the future is precisely predictable.

Useful elements:

- Historical revenue
- Burn
- Cash
- Runway
- Gross margin
- Hiring assumptions
- Major operating drivers
- Scenario range

Andreessen Horowitz recommends historical P&L and burn as core diligence information.

Source:

- https://a16z.com/the-insiders-guide-to-data-rooms-what-to-know-before-you-raise/

DocSend’s 2026 guidance favors realistic projections over implausible hockey-stick forecasts.

Source:

- https://www.docsend.com/blog/what-vcs-really-want-to-see-inside-your-seed-deck/

---

### 9.14 Fundraising ask

The ask is a milestone story. The single best framing question is:

> Where does this round take the company?

To answer it, the slide should cover:

- How much are you raising?
- What runway does it provide?
- What milestones will it achieve?
- What will be true at the next financing that is not true today?

Techstars’ 2026-05-07 guidance recommends framing the raise around the milestones the money enables, not simply percentage allocation to departments.

Source:

- https://www.techstars.com/blog/founder-advice/why-most-pitch-decks-dont-work-and-how-to-make-sure-yours-does

#### Strong ask

> Raising $3M to reach $4M ARR, launch the enterprise product, and prove <12-month CAC payback

#### Weaker ask

> 50% engineering / 30% sales / 20% operations

#### Worked contrast

Instead of:

> We are raising $3M for 50% engineering, 30% GTM, 20% operations.

Use:

> We are raising $3M to reach $4M ARR, establish repeatable enterprise sales, ship the compliance platform, and reach Series A with 24 months of operating capacity.

The second version names runway, repeatability, and the state of the company at the next financing.

The departmental percentages can live in the appendix.

---

### 9.15 Vision

Sequoia recommends articulating what the company can become over the long term.

Source:

- https://sequoiacap.com/article/writing-a-business-plan/

The final strategic slide should answer:

> If this succeeds, what important company exists in five or ten years?

The vision should be larger than the current feature set but logically connected to the initial wedge.

---

# Type and layout

Text density, the type scale, font choice and compatibility, the grid, alignment, and the reusable layouts they imply.

## Text Density

Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health recommends:

- Text used sparingly
- Lists limited to roughly **2-4 items**
- Continuous text blocks limited to roughly **two lines**
- Generous white space
- Headline-oriented slide structure

Source:

- https://hsph.harvard.edu/research/health-communication/resources/slide-checklist/

### Practical default

For live decks:

- 1 headline
- 0-3 short supporting lines
- 1 visual or data display
- 1 source line, at the live floor

For read-alone decks:

- 1 headline
- 1 short explanatory sentence
- 1-3 evidence points
- 1 visual/data element
- 1 source line, at the read-alone floor

### Avoid

- Paragraphs
- 8-12 bullet points
- Full sentences read aloud verbatim
- Text boxes spread randomly around the slide
- Important information hidden in a footnote below the floor for the mode

### Where the explanation goes

Text you cut from a slide still has to live somewhere, and where depends on the mode.

- Live deck: the speaker notes. You are in the room, so you say it out loud.
- Read-alone deck: the appendix. An emailed PDF carries no narration, so notes nobody opens are not a cure.

#### Enforced (see SKILL.md)

At live-deck type sizes the word limit is close to a physical limit anyway: 40
words of on-slide text (JUDGMENT), and at most six visible objects. That object
budget is one headline plus zero to three lines plus one visual. Harvard's
2-to-4-item lists and two-line text blocks are the shape that budget produces.

The audit counts **table cells and chart category labels as on-slide text**,
because a dense table is the commonest place a paragraph hides.

---

## Typography

### Source-backed guidance

Harvard accessibility guidance recommends sans-serif fonts and at least **18 pt** for slide presentations.

Source:

- https://accessibility.huit.harvard.edu/microsoft-powerpoint

Stanford recommends 24 pt or larger sans-serif type for visible presentation slides.

Source:

- https://oralcommprogram.stanford.edu/presentation-and-delivery/visuals-and-powerpoint

Harvard T.H. Chan's slide checklist recommends approximately:

- **28 pt** headline
- **18-24 pt** body

Source:

- https://hsph.harvard.edu/research/health-communication/resources/slide-checklist/

These are institutional minimum/guideline values, not maximums.

They describe type read across a room, so they govern the live table below. That is why the read-alone table can sit below Stanford's 24 pt without contradicting it: an emailed deck is read at arm's length on a screen the reader controls.

### Practical startup-deck typography

The middle column is the range. The right column is the single value to put in the slide master if you do not want to think about it.

#### Live presentation

| Element | Recommended range | Pick these |
|---|---:|---:|
| Hero number | 48-80+ pt | 60-72 pt Bold |
| Main headline | 36-54 pt | 42 pt Semibold |
| Subheadline or supporting heading | 28-36 pt | 28 pt Regular |
| Body | 24-30 pt | 24 pt Regular |
| Labels and chart labels | 18-24 pt | 20 pt Medium |
| Source/footer | 18 pt floor | 18 pt Regular |

#### Sent/read-alone deck

| Element | Recommended range | Pick these |
|---|---:|---:|
| Hero number | 40-64 pt | 48-60 pt Bold |
| Main headline | 30-44 pt | 36 pt Semibold |
| Subheadline or supporting heading | 24-32 pt | 24 pt Regular |
| Body | 20-26 pt | 22 pt Regular |
| Labels and chart labels | 16-20 pt | 18 pt Medium |
| Source/footer | 14 pt floor | 14 pt Regular |

The pick-these values are practical defaults derived from the institutional minimums and live-presentation guidance above. Two notes on them:

- The weights are part of the default: semibold headline, regular body and subheadline, medium labels.
- An older draft of this file used 26 pt for the live subheadline and 12-16 pt for source lines. Both sat below the range or the floor for their mode, so they are raised here: 28 pt and 18 pt live, 14 pt read-alone.

#### Rule

If important information only fits below the floor for the mode, the slide contains too much. Cut the content, do not shrink the type.

#### Enforced (see SKILL.md)

18 pt is a hard floor for a live deck and 14 pt for a read-alone one: the audit
fails on any run below it, including inside tables. The 18 pt live floor is
Harvard accessibility guidance. The 14 pt read-alone floor is a judgment of this
skill, not Harvard.

The audit also fails a slide whose *largest* text is under 36 pt on a live deck, or 30 pt on a read-alone deck, which catches a
slide with no hierarchy at all. And it fails a slide whose largest-to-smallest
ratio is under 1.8x, which catches a slide where everything is the same size and
nothing says what matters.

The source line stays on the slide, set at the floor for the mode. Only overflow
provenance, meaning the full citation, the methodology and the sample sizes,
moves to the appendix. A live projected deck is the one case where the visible
line can go, because the presenter says the provenance out loud.

---

## Font Selection

Microsoft accessibility guidance favors simple, familiar fonts and recommends avoiding overly decorative or difficult-to-read styles.

Source:

- https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/accessibility/powerpoint/make-your-powerpoint-presentations-accessible-to-people-with-disabilities

### Good general choices

#### High compatibility

- Aptos
- Arial
- Calibri
- Segoe UI

#### Common professional choices

- Inter
- Helvetica or Helvetica Neue
- Avenir
- Source Sans
- IBM Plex Sans
- Neue Haas Grotesk
- Similar highly legible sans-serif families

### How many families

One sans-serif family is the default. A second family only with a reason you can say in a sentence, and two is the ceiling. An optional monospace for code or technical identifiers does not spend the second slot.

One family carries the whole deck through weight:

- **Bold/Semibold** for headlines
- **Medium** for labels
- **Regular** for body
- Optional Mono for code and technical identifiers only

### Avoid

- A second family with no reason, and any third family at all (the optional monospace does not count toward the two)
- Ultra-light body type
- Condensed body type
- Excessive italics
- Underlining as decoration
- Decorative script/display fonts
- Large amounts of ALL CAPS

---

## Font Compatibility and Embedding

Microsoft explains that font embedding can preserve layout when recipients do not have a custom font installed. It recommends embedding all characters when others may edit the file.

Source:

- https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/benefits-of-embedding-custom-fonts-cb3982aa-ea76-4323-b008-86670f222dbc

### Practical recommendation

For a pitch:

- Keep a version using broadly available fonts.
- If using a custom font in `.pptx`, embed it where licensing permits.
- Always test the deck on a second computer.
- Export a PDF before sending externally.
- Check whether text reflows after export.

---

## Aspect Ratio and Slide Dimensions

Microsoft states that 16:9 widescreen is the default for new PowerPoint presentations and describes widescreen as the best choice for presentations because it provides more slide surface.

Official widescreen dimensions:

- **33.867 x 19.05 cm**
- Aspect ratio: 16:9

Source:

- https://support.microsoft.com/en-US/PowerPoint/change-the-size-of-your-powerpoint-slides

### Recommendation

Treat 16:9 as the strong default, not a requirement. Named exceptions:

- A conference requires 4:3
- A specific venue gives another format
- You are designing a printable document rather than a presentation

Do not resize the deck near the end of the process; changing aspect ratio can cause layout problems.

---

## Layout and Grid

A pitch deck should feel designed as one system.

Standardize:

- Left/right margins
- Top headline position
- Line spacing
- Section spacing
- Font system
- Logo position
- Footer/source style
- Number formatting
- Chart style
- Image corner treatment
- Color meaning

One footer and source style, used on every slide that carries data.
